solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Escape Mandelson's inner primitive being

indicators.note: inner points to letters lying inside the run of words, spanning the gap between them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word into the start of the name

explanation.surface: Peter Mandelson is urged to set free his inner caveman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Escape' looks like a verb addressed to Mandelson, but its last three letters start the answer, which continues into the politician's name.
explanation.definitionFit: An ape-man is a hominid halfway between ape and human, the textbook picture of a primitive creature.

clue.text: Police backing rubbish alternative oppressor

indicators.note: going backing means moving in the rear direction, so the letters run back to front

parts.note: the Criminal Investigation Department, Britain's plain-clothes detectives
tat is cheap tawdry stuff
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: Police support a rubbish rival to a tyrant, a jab at heavy-handed government.
explanation.walkthrough: CID is the detective branch of British police forces; turned round it opens the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dictator rules with absolute power and typically crushes opposition, making him a classic tyrant.

clue.text: (& 19dn.) Trump's hardly a fan of this liberal crowd

definitions.text: Trump's hardly a fan of this

parts.note: liberal in the sense of open-handed or unrestricted
a crowd can be described as a crush of people, as when bodies are jammed together, and the same word means to push

explanation.surface: Trump has little love for this liberal mob, a dig at his media enemies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal crowd' reads as a sneer at progressives, but it splits into two plain synonyms; the definition is the whole opening description.
explanation.definitionFit: Trump routinely attacks independent newspapers and broadcasters as fake news, so an unfettered media is something he dislikes.

clue.text: In danger of being an heretical martyr?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: at risk, liable to be lost
second meaning, literal: tied to the post where heretics were burned

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second reading as playful: heretics were burned while bound to a wooden post.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for something under threat is the same phrase as the physical position of a burning victim tied to the post.

clue.text: Potty material — Carter to a T, sadly

indicators.note: things that go sadly go wrong, so the letters end up in a disordered arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is daft about Carter, matching him exactly, which is a sorry state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potty' looks like mad, but it means of pots: the definition is clay used to make flowerpots.
explanation.definitionFit: Terracotta is the brownish-red fired clay from which flowerpots and other pottery are commonly made.

clue.text: A book on bastard Boris — one must go and suck up!

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a bastard form is corrupted or impure, so the letters appear in a debased order
one is the Roman numeral, and must go says to drop it

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for book
the name taken as written, before trimming

explanation.surface: A book attacks Boris Johnson; one ought to leave, and toady to him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suck up' reads as grovel, but here it means soak in. One is I, removed from the name before the rest is jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: To absorb is to take in liquid, just as a sponge soaks or draws up water.

clue.text: In other words, the EU makes Boris's and Trump's countries less awful

parts.note: Boris's country is Britain, abbreviated BR

indicators.note: awful means dreadful or messed up, so these letters come out in a poor order

parts.note: Trump's country is the United States
taken as written

explanation.surface: The European Union apparently makes Johnson's Britain and Trump's America look less terrible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Countries' is shared by both leaders: one supplies BR for Britain, the other US.
explanation.definitionFit: The Belgian capital houses the main EU institutions, so the city's name is used as shorthand for the Union itself.

clue.text: Main concern is outrageous Tory rip-off, 'embracing independence'

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in the arms, so one piece wraps around another
something outrageous is wild and out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the -off joining in the surface only
I is the standard abbreviation for independent or independence

explanation.surface: The chief worry is a scandalous Conservative swindle dressed up as freedom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rip-off' looks like one noun, but only the first half is fodder; the jumbled letters then wrap round the single letter for independence.
explanation.definitionFit: A priority is the thing given most importance, the matter that comes first among one's worries.

clue.text: What's left, after getting married, for Dick?

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for married
an ember is what remains of a fire once it has burnt down

explanation.surface: A rueful question: what remains for poor Dick once he has wed?
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the remains of a fire after the marriage abbreviation. 'Dick' looks like a man's name, but it is slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are vulgar or euphemistic slang words for the penis, so the crude term matches the polite one.

clue.text: (& 27dn.) Flak — Oppostion gets sack

parts.note: the opposing side in a war
to sack someone is to dismiss them from a job

explanation.surface: The Opposition takes criticism and then is dismissed, like a political leader under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opposition' looks like the parliamentary party, but it just means the other side in a battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Flak is anti-aircraft gunfire, shells shot by hostile forces at aircraft overhead.

clue.text: Rotten teeth on ma (decayed)

indicators.note: something decayed has crumbled and broken down, so the letters are rebuilt in a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Mum's teeth have gone bad, as the bracketed comment drily notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rotten' sits beside 'teeth' as a natural adjective but is the definition; the bracketed word, looking like a gloss, is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Moth-eaten describes cloth chewed by moth larvae, and figuratively anything shabby, worn out and decrepit.

clue.text: Is encouraging bounders to protect Tory leader

indicators.note: protecting means shielding on all sides, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: roos are kangaroos, animals that bound along

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cynical aside: someone cheers on cads so that they shield the Conservative leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounders' looks like the old word for cads, but here they are things that bound: kangaroos, shortened to roos.
explanation.definitionFit: To root for a team is an idiom for cheering it on, so the third person form means is supporting.

clue.text: Tip: when pissed and stuck in jail, complain

indicators.note: something stuck in sits inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: the nick is British slang for prison

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunk letters stagger out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice: if you are drunk and locked up, have a moan about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' looks like a heading for advice, but it is the fodder; in British slang pissed means drunk and the nick is jail.
explanation.definitionFit: To nitpick is to find fault over petty details, a fussy kind of grumbling or criticising.

clue.text: Ignorant of Dicky having stress

parts.note: dicky is British slang for weak or unwell, as in a dicky heart
to iterate is to say again, a way of emphasising a point

explanation.surface: Someone unaware that a man called Dicky is under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' looks like a name, but it is British slang meaning poorly or unsound.
explanation.definitionFit: Illiterate means unable to read, and more broadly uneducated or lacking knowledge in some field.

clue.text: Grim mark of authority, seizing a 'brother'

indicators.note: to seize is to grab and hold, so one piece is gripped inside another

parts.note: a ceremonial mace is carried as a symbol of authority
taken as written
BR is the abbreviation for brother

explanation.surface: A stern symbol of power grabs a supposed comrade, something sinister in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The quote marks round 'brother' hint at a union comrade, but it simply gives its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Macabre means gruesome and dwelling on death, close to the sense of grim as ghastly and forbidding.

clue.text: Threat of Cyclops hacking computer language

indicators.note: hacking into a system means breaking in, so one piece gets inside another

parts.note: Perl is a programming language
the setter refers to himself, so his name stands for the first person pronoun

explanation.surface: The risk posed by the setter breaking into a coding language.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is this puzzle's setter, so naming him gives the pronoun I, slipped into the programming language's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A peril is a serious danger or risk, which is what a threat is.

clue.text: see 23ac.
Boris colleague? Pack up

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a surname, that of a minister who served in Boris Johnson's cabinet
second meaning: to bind or tie up tightly, as with poultry

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: Liz Truss was Foreign Secretary under Boris Johnson before succeeding him.
explanation.definitionFit: The politician's surname is also a verb meaning to tie up tightly, as a cook binds a chicken for roasting.

clue.text: Marriage: it's out for the politician

parts.note: a marriage is a union of two people

indicators.note: out can mean out of place or wrong, so the letters are put out of order

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Wedlock is off the table for this particular politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's out' reads as marriage being ruled out, but 'out' is jumbling the two-word contraction.
explanation.definitionFit: A Unionist is a politician supporting the union of Northern Ireland, or Scotland, with Great Britain.

clue.text: see 3dn.
Mailer's sperm shaken about in the morning

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is placed round another
shaking something mixes it up, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
a.m. denotes the morning

explanation.surface: A crude jibe at the novelist Norman Mailer's virility being tested early in the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mailer' looks like the American writer, but it means someone who sends mail; 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A spammer sends unsolicited bulk email, so he is a sender of mail on an industrial scale.

clue.text: Fairer to take lead from scoundrel?

indicators.note: taking the lead away removes whatever stands at the very front

parts.note: blighter is British slang for a rotter

explanation.surface: Asking whether it would be more just to let a rogue go first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fairer' reads as more just, but the definition means paler or less dark in colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair hair or skin is light in colour, so the comparative forms are synonyms in that sense.

clue.text: Privileged people's unfinished convenience by railway

indicators.note: something unfinished lacks its ending, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: the gents is a British men's public lavatory, a convenience
RY is an abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: The upper classes have a half-built toilet next to the railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: A public convenience is a toilet; the British name for the men's one loses its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The gentry are the landed class just below the nobility, a socially advantaged group.

clue.text: (& 16dn.) Putting party's interests before the electorate and collapsing — pity I snapped

definitions.text: Putting party's interests before the electorate

indicators.note: something snapped is broken apart, so the letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A government that puts party before voters falls apart, and the narrator loses patience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collapsing' looks like an anagram signal but is part of the fodder; the signal is the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing politics means acting for partisan advantage rather than the public good, the cynical choice described.

clue.text: Fergal O'Shea's centre for waterproof footwear

indicators.note: the centre is the middle portion, so the letters lie within the words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first name into the surname

explanation.surface: The heart of an Irishman named Fergal O'Shea is good for rain boots.
explanation.walkthrough: The name is invented to carry the letters; the apostrophe in the surname is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A galosh is a rubber overshoe worn over ordinary shoes to keep them dry in wet weather.

clue.text: Casual Blair's cosying up to right is "cosmetic"

indicators.note: cosying up to means snuggling close beside, so one piece sits next to another

parts.note: Tone is the familiar shortening of Tony Blair's first name
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: An informal Tony Blair snuggling up to the right wing is mere window dressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' looks like the political right Blair courted, but it just gives its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Toner is a skincare liquid applied to the face after cleansing, a beauty product.

clue.text: Amin's life: scattering big game

indicators.note: scattering spreads things in all directions, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Idi Amin's life story: dispersing large wild animals, a hunting dictator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big game' looks like hunted animals in Africa, beside the Ugandan dictator, but it means an important match.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi-final is the penultimate round of a tournament, an important sporting fixture.

clue.text: see 10dn.
Minister (rogue!) put away

parts.note: a cur is a contemptible man
to put away food is to eat it

explanation.surface: A government minister, a scoundrel, is locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' looks like a government office, but it is a clergyman; 'put away' means eaten, not jailed.
explanation.definitionFit: A curate is an assistant priest, and minister is a general word for a clergyman.

clue.text: New non-British money is causing mental disturbance

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
the currency of the eurozone, which Britain never adopted
taken as written

explanation.surface: A new foreign currency is driving Brexit-minded Britons to anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: Britain kept the pound, so the single European currency is money that is not British.
explanation.definitionFit: A neurosis is a mild mental illness marked by anxiety or obsession, a psychological disorder.
